Article Title: Akash Deep sizzles, Jasprit Bumrah struggles as New Zealand frustrate India on Day 1
Article Text:

India's Akash Deep, right, is congratulated by teammates after taking the wicket of New Zealand's Tom Latham during play on day one of the second cricket test between New Zealand and India in Christchurch, New Zealand, Friday.

Brief Scores

Twenty-two balls, three wickets and no addition to the scoreboard. The passage of play injected life back into India's bowling, and it was that man Akash Deep again. With the old ball, he found the right length for this surface, which still had enough bite to keep the bowlers interested. There was no magic formula for the Hagley Oval strip, and attacking the stumps while making the batter play was always going to test the batters."Pitch was fresh. The first session had more moisture, so edges didn't carry. We bowled in better areas in the second session and it worked. Pitch will get better if the sun remains out," he told reporters after the end of Day 1."The plan was to make the batter play, it was self-realisation. I wanted to make the batter play 90 per cent of the times. Ball was moving a lot in the first session," he added.After making the new ball talk and finding Tom Latham's edge (which KL Rahul grassed in the slips), Akash made the subtle adjustment to negate the extra bounce by going a touch fuller. The around-the-wicket angle against left-handers further planted seeds of doubt in the batters, who had no option but to play the line and get undone by enough movement off the pitch.Tom Latham was the first to fall to the plan, Rachin Ravindra followed in the next over during his spell, and an Anshul Kamboj breakthrough in between reduced the hosts from 110/1 to 110/4. In the space of 16 deliveries, three batters were back in the hut, and the relentlessness of the two fast bowlers paid off after they toiled hard in the first session.Akash, India's most threatening bowler on the day, bowled seven overs with decent pace. The figures read 7-4-7-2, and he could easily have taken a couple more wickets. He didn't get carried away by the bounce off the Day 1 strip and just stuck to the basics: hitting the same spot and subtly using the width of the crease to play with angles. Most importantly, he intended to make the batter play, which was key on a surface that had less grass compared to what we saw at the Basin Reserve in Wellington earlier this week."Overall, a good day, but we could have done better. We were discussing yesterday that this pitch is better than Basin Reserve," Akash said.From the other end, during different periods of play, debutant Gurnoor Brar bowled with pace and made effective use of the short ball. Anshul Kamboj sprayed it around with the new ball, but his spell with Akash after lunch put the hosts under pressure.Introduced late into the attack, Washington Sundar got rid of dangerman Daryl Mitchell for 31, but another lower-order partnership, between Tom Blundell and Glenn Phillips, frustrated the visitors, who started playing the waiting game for the second new ball. Shubman Gill turned to his most successful bowler of the day, Akash, and Bumrah for the first crack with the red cherry, but New Zealand did well to negate that period.At stumps, Blundell and Phillips remained unbeaten, with the scoreboard reading 246/5.However, it was Jasprit Bumrah 's performance that will give India's management a thing or two to think about. Bumrah, the ace in the pack, had a rather underwhelming day, where he went past the bat, found some edges but returned wicketless. It has been over 200 balls since he last picked up a wicket in the series. He used an unusual run-up and load-up during his spell after Tea; it wasn't the usual way he held the ball, and his hands weren't in the position we've seen for over a decade now."Jasprit Bumrah was practising that run-up in practice also. Jasprit Bumrah hai wo, kuch soch ke hi kar rahe hoge (He's Jasprit Bumrah, after all. He must be doing it after giving it some thought)."The speed gun flirted around the 130 kph mark, and there was visible frustration with his trademark kick to the surface every time he went past the bat. Maybe it wasn't his day, but he was far from the menacing best we have seen in the past. Since the first over of the second New Zealand innings at the Basin, where he dismissed Tom Latham for a duck off the second delivery, the fast bowler has been searching for a wicket.New Zealand: 246/5 after 85 overs (Tom Blundell 53 batting, Tom Latham 59; Akash Deep 2/52)

The around-the-wicket angle against left-handers further planted seeds of doubt in the batters, who had no option but to play the line.

Article Title: 'Winning habit': Sjoerd Marijne on India's rise to world No. 4
Article Text:
For Sjoerd Marijne, the remarkable rise has been built on hard work, discipline and a growing belief within a side where, as he puts it, “winning becomes a habit”.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: When Sjoerd Marijne took charge of the Indian women’s hockey team in Jan, they were ranked ninth in the world after having finished 2025 in 10th place. Even he did not expect them to climb to No. 4 before the year was over.But that’s exactly what happened after India registered their fifth win at the ongoing Asian Champions Trophy against Japan in Bhopal on Wednesday, extending their winning run to 13 matches across three tournaments, starting with the World Cup, and earning their best-ever world ranking.For Marijne, the remarkable rise has been built on hard work, discipline and a growing belief within a side where, as he puts it, “winning becomes a habit”.“We did our calculations before the tournament and knew that if we won all the matches, we could go to No. 5. No. 4, I didn’t expect,” said Marijne during an exclusive interview with TOI on Thursday.“It has been a whole process, step by step, and coming so close to the top three is unique and amazing for us.”Marijne, though, is reluctant to take the credit for the turnaround himself, stressing that the rise has been a collective effort extending well beyond the players and coaching staff, from the groundsman at SAI Bengaluru to those working behind the scenes at Hockey India.However, there is no single aspect that Marijne believes has transformed the team. He sees the progress as the result of a combination of qualities, particularly the discipline to maintain standards even when playing lower-ranked opposition.“Besides that, we are really enjoying what we are doing. You can see that in the girls. They have really become a unit, with a lot of respect for each other. They work hard, but they also work for each other,” he added.Marijne has also consciously tried to create an atmosphere that allows players and staff to switch between intense professionalism and lighter moments, whether that means joking together, playing musical chairs or dancing on the team bus after matches.“We are very serious, we are very disciplined, but we also have a lot of fun among the staff and with the girls,” he said. “Life is too short to only be serious. We also need to laugh with each other and enjoy what we’re doing.”The coach also believes the increasing consistency against teams India are expected to beat is an important indication of their development.“We are getting more dominant. We have a very good winning mindset, and we need to get to a stage where winning becomes a habit,” he said.While the rankings underline how far India have come, Marijne is already measuring the team against a much bigger objective: the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.“We know exactly how we want to have the team at the Olympics in 2028. We look at where we were, where we want to go and where we are now,” he said. “The benchmark at the Olympics is very high.”The Pro League next year will therefore be less about an isolated tournament and more about another stage in India’s Olympic preparation.“For us, the Pro League is preparation for the Olympics,” said the Dutchman. “Those are matches where we can try things, try players in different positions, try more players and see how they play against the best seven or eight countries in the world.”With the Hockey India League coming before the international assignments in Argentina and India, Marijne expects managing the transition to provide another test for the squad. He also plans to take the team to Chile for a few matches before the Argentina leg.But for now, his focus is on defending the Asian Champions Trophy title, with the climb to No. 4 doing little to alter the central message he keeps giving his players.“We are raising the bar,” he said. “It’s good what we have done, but we also show them what needs to be better.”
Article Summary: Sjoerd Marijne took charge of the Indian women’s hockey team in Jan. They were ranked ninth in the world after having finished 2025 in 10th place. India registered their fifth win at the ongoing Asian Champions Trophy against Japan in Bhopal on Wednesday.

Article Title: 'Nostalgic opening from lockdown days': Gukesh explains London System choice
Article Text:
Image credit: FIDE

D Gukesh, with white, was not really happy about a soft draw one that allowed Javokhir Sindarov equality and almost forced another draw with repetition of moves.The second game of the 14-game World Chess Championship match between the Indian champion and Uzbek challenger ended in a peace treaty inside two hours and just 20 moves of the London System opening (3.Bf4) in Geneva on Wednesday. Except a knight each, the other 30 pieces were on the board (15 each) when the game ended tamely.Before coming out of the players’ lounge to the fan zone and to the press conference, Gukesh was in a mood of self reflection and did not appear happy with how things had panned out despite having the advantage of white pieces. But he regrouped quickly and managed more than a smile while giving a quick reaction to the official broadcast and detailed answers at the media conference.“Away from the board, I have been much happier compared to Singapore (the match against Ding Liren in 2024),” said Gukesh.On how different it is to be at the match without his father accompanying him and instead, with his Bengaluru-based designer friends Shikhar and Charmie, Gukesh said, “Being with friends takes away a lot of the stress. Happy they are here. Also Gayo (second Gajewski) is here and is doing a lot of work.Happy with the setup for this match.”Gukesh opting for the London system is not suspect, but has been played only twice in World Championship matches (Ding beat Nepo in 2022 and Gukesh and Ding split a point in 2024). Though the opening was a mild surprise, Sindarov was up to the task and on the Uzbek’s prepared line (7..Qb6), Gukesh laughed, “I could not recollect what I was doing here. I felt I could have remembered more from my notes ... It was my nostalgic opening from the lockdown days. ”“There is a lot of theory in London (system) too. But it was not some deep strategy (to play this).”Gukesh explained that the position was such that he could always hope that Sindarov could go wrong had they continued to play (and avoid three-fold repetition) but it's likely that even he himself could go wrong and there was not much in the position.Black’s 15th move (f5) invited a long thought from Gukesh and after about 30 minutes he responded with f3 and fell about 35 minutes behind needing to make 24 more moves in about 50 mins. Earlier, a new position on the board was reached after Sindarov's queen retreat (Qd8) on the 11th move.The third game will be played on Thursday before Friday’s rest day with Gukesh having black pieces.Moves (Game 2):D Gukesh vs Javokhir Sindarov -- 1. d4 d5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Bf4 c5 4. e3 e6 5. Nbd2 Nc6 6. c3 Be7 7. Ne5 Qb6 8. Rb1 Nxe5 9. Bxe5 Bd7 10. a4 O-O 11. Bd3 Qd8 12. O-O Rc8 13. Ra1 Be8 14. Qe2 Nd7 15. Bg3 f5 16. f3 Nf6 17. Be5 Nd7 18. Bg3 Nf6 19. Be5 Nd7 20. Bg3 Nf6.Game drawn

Article Title: Treesa Jolly-Gayatri Gopichand duo begins title defence with easy win
Article Text:
Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand

LUCKNOW: Defending champions Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand began their bid for a hat-trick of titles with a comfortable victory as Indian shuttlers made a strong start to the Syed Modi India International Super 300 badminton on Wednesday.The World Championships bronze medallists brushed aside qualifiers Rashmi Ganesh and Amrutha Pramuthesh 21-8, 21-7 in the opening round.Speaking about the playing conditions, Treesa said the pair took some time to adjust in their opening match.“The conditions were slow and slightly tricky. In the second game, our opponents also played some good rallies and challenged us. We stayed patient, played longer rallies and tried to understand the court and atmosphere better since it was our first match,” she said.Gayatri, meanwhile, said the crowd support in Lucknow had given the pair an added boost.“We have received tremendous support from the crowd, and that gives us a lot of confidence.”
Article Summary: Defending champions Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand beat Rashmi Ganesh and Amrutha Pramuthesh 21-8, 21-7 in the opening round of the Syed Modi India International Super 300 badminton tournament.

Article Title: Mrithika’s golden run continues at BIMSTEC meet
Article Text:
Mrithika

KOLKATA: Mrithika T continued her brilliant showing this year as she won the women’s 100m gold on the opening day of the BIMSTEC Under-23 Athletics Meet at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar.Mrithika, hailing from Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu, clocked 12.02s to narrowly edge past Sri Lanka’s K. Risansa Hirupama (12.07s). Bangladesh’s Dewan Sumaya (12.24s) won bronze. Interestingly, the 17-year-old wasn’t initially selected for the individual 100m, so naturally her coach was more than happy after she finished on top of the podium on Wednesday.“I didn’t even know she would be running the 100m here. Until yesterday, I only knew that she had been selected for the 4x100m relay. We hadn’t prepared specifically for the 100m, so I’m very happy that she won the gold medal,” said coach Parthiban.As for Mrithika, who broke the 100m meet record at the National Youth Championships in September (11.78s) and then clocked a lifetime best of 11.71s at the National Junior Championships in Oct, she couldn’t have been more excited.“I want to thank my coach, who has supported me right from the beginning, and my father.He has always supported me and has been my backbone. If he wasn’t there, I wouldn’t be here today,” said the Class XII student of Brindhavan Vidhyalaya Public School in Coimbatore.It was her father, Thirugnanajothi, who inspired Mrithika to take up the sport, and he still makes sure to drop her off for her 5am training sessions. “My mother also gets up very early in the morning to prepare my diet and food. My parents have done so much for me, and I’m very thankful to them,” she added.Besides Mrithika, India won five more gold medals on the opening day.Among the men, Anurag Singh Kaler won the shot put with a throw of 18.34m, Daksh Bishnoi won the triple jump with a leap of 15.58m, while Hitesh clinched the 1500m title.Among the women, Priya (52.03m) and Nikita Kumari (50.02m) led an Indian one-two in the discus throw. In the final race of the day, the women’s 5000m, India’s Sonam Parmar (17:31.12) and Sunita Devi (17:31.66) fought a tight race to win gold and silver, respectively.Sri Lanka’s K. Niduki Prarthana (17:47.07) was third.Sri Lanka, meanwhile, won two gold medals, with Dineth Induwara Weraratna claiming the men’s 100m title in 10.35s. India’s Rushiprasad Desai (10.46s) finished second, while Sri Lanka’s Saad Jamaldeen (10.57s) also made the podium.Nethya Sampath Jonikku won the other gold for the island nation in the high jump with a leap of 2.08m, while India’s Binoy B and Ambriesh K, who also cleared 2.08m, finished second and third, respectively.
Article Summary: Mrithika T won the women's 100m gold on the opening day of the BIMSTEC Under-23 Athletics Meet at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar. The 17-year-old, hailing from Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu, clocked 12.02s to narrowly edge past Sri Lanka’s K. Risansa Hirupama (12.07s)

Article Title: AFC Champions League: Jeakson’s late strike fuels East Bengal’s knockout hopes
Article Text:
Jeakson Singh (second from right) scores East Bengal’s winner against Al-Hussein at Salt Lake Stadium.

KOLKATA: Sometimes, football defies logic. East Bengal FC’s historic 1-0 win against Jordanian champions Al-Hussein SC in the reverse fixture of their AFC Champions League Two clash here on Tuesday — a first by an Indian club since the continent’s second-tier club tournament was rebranded in 2024 — was one such moment.After living on the edge for most of the contest and getting rescued by the woodwork four times, East Bengal somehow flipped the script. They earned a corner in the 87th minute — their first in the second session — and Bashim Rashid whipped in a well-measured delivery towards the first post. David Lalhlansanga deftly placed the ball in front of Jeakson Singh, who fired home.After two draws and two losses, East Bengal kept their hopes of advancing to the round of 16 alive with this win. They will travel to face Group D leaders Al Shorta of Iraq on Dec. 8. Only the top two from each group will make the knockouts.
Article Summary: East Bengal FC beat Jordanian champions Al-Hussein SC 1-0. Jeakson Singh scored the winner in the 87th minute at Salt Lake Stadium. It was the first AFC Champions League Two win by an Indian club since the continent’s second-tier club tournament was rebranded in 2024.

Article Title: ‘ICC, boards need to step in’: Harbhajan Singh on India-Pakistan cricket skirmishes
Article Text:
Harbhajan Singh has joined the chorus of those voicing their concern at the deteriorating player behaviour during India-Pakistan clashes.

'Have some patience with Team India'

MUMBAI: The last couple of India-Pakistan cricket contests, while they've provided plenty of excitement, have also seen ugly scenes of skirmishes between the players. On November 14, India's Under-19 players had a go at their Pakistani counterparts, celebrating wildly and overenthusiastically after pipping their arch-rivals by one wicket in a thrilling Under-19 Asia Cup final at Al Amerat in Oman. On November 22 (Sunday) in Doha, players of both India A and Pakistan A (Pakistani Shaheens) exchanged verbal volleys with each other, with India A pacer Harshit Rana involved in heated altercations with the Pakistan players during their Asia Cup Rising Stars match in Doha, which Pakistan A won by 48 runs.After the ugly scenes witnessed in the Asia Cup Under-19 final, former India skipper Dilip Vengsarkar had told TOI about the need for the BCCI to educate young cricketers at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence about behaving well on the field while playing for India at any level. India's off-spin great Harbhajan Singh has joined the chorus of those voicing their concern at the deteriorating player behaviour during these clashes and has urged the game's authorities — the International Cricket Council and the BCCI — to "step in" to check the trend of players from both countries getting carried away in Indo-Pak cricket matches."Somewhere down the line, the ICC needs to step in. I think it is just getting a bit too much with the reactions. First, Pakistan's boys did it (after beating India Under-19s in the league stage). Then the Indians won and did it. And then yesterday too, whatever happened was not right. If you look at sport as a sport, then it will be far better. See, some amount of chit chat happens, and has been happening for a long time. That should happen also.The game needs a bit of masala (spice) like that. However, it should not reach a point where you feel it is shameful. So, somewhere down the line, I think that the ICC and the respective boards need to put their foot forward and say, 'this is not done.' 'You try hard on the field to win the match for your team, try your best, but after the match, those reactions, I don't think are the right ones. Both from our side and their side," Harbhajan told reporters at an event at the BPGC Golf Course here on Tuesday.Asked specifically about Rana's on-field clashes with Pakistan's players, Harbhajan quipped, "I don't think that should happen. I think it is not setting the right example for the generation coming up."While he wasn't critical of India's bowlers' inability to take New Zealand's eight remaining wickets on the final day of the first Test at Wellington, which ended in a draw on Monday, calling the pitch "really flat," Harbhajan, who took 417 wickets in 103 Tests (1998-2015), wasn't entirely convinced about India's decision to shake hands with their Kiwi counterparts even with 15 overs left to be bowled in the last session of the match, and felt that they could have continued bowling. "I thought the pitch was dry and very flat. It's okay. Pitches in Australia and New Zealand tend to be really flat, at times.“I think a lot has been talked about in this game. There were 15 overs left and they declared the game (a draw) before. Yes, you could have tried. You never know. Things move very fast in cricket. But somewhere down the line, you have to be honest with yourself, as a captain and management, whether it was the right decision on that pitch or in that scenario. I think that a lot of thought would have gone into that decision. But if I was part of the management, I would have liked to bowl another 15 overs and give it a try. And let's see. You never know,” Harbhajan said.Recalling how former Australia captain Michael Clarke, with his part-time left-arm spin, had bowled Australia to a win against India in the closing minutes of the controversial Sydney Test in January 2008, taking three for five in 1.5 overs, the former tweaker said, "After everyone else had bowled, Australia introduced Clarke just two overs before (the close of the Test). And nothing was happening. Suddenly he came and he took those two important wickets and they ended up winning that match. So, cricket is a very funny game. Anything can happen."Citing the fighting attitude of his former India spin-bowling partner and ex-India captain Anil Kumble, Harbhajan said, "I have always been a fan of Anil Bhai. And I still say that his attitude was that you have to fight till the last ball. Whether you are bowling or batting or in the field, you have to fight till the last ball. So 90 balls is a lot. I think we should have tried in those 90 balls (to get the remaining five Kiwi wickets). You never know. Maybe the result will come in your favour."Harbhajan defended off-spinner Washington Sundar, who took one for 65 in 35 overs as the Kiwis secured a draw in the first Test. "It's very easy for all of us to pinpoint an individual and say he could have done this or he could have done that. I will put myself in his position. He tried his best. He is young. He is learning. And of course, the more he plays, the more he will learn about these situations. Next time, if he is in such a situation, I am sure he will be able to perform better. So, let's not pinpoint an individual. You win with 11, you lose with 11 and you throw with 11. He must have tried. If it was me, I would have tried as well. So, give him some time. I am sure he will learn and he will get better," Harbhajan stressed.Critics have panned India's inability to close out Test wins in their last two games by taking wickets on the fifth and final day — it happened against Sri Lanka in Colombo in August, and then against New Zealand on the final day of the first Test at Wellington. Harbhajan, though, isn't perturbed and urged fans to "have some patience with the Indian team.""That will happen (closing out Test wins). This is the same team that won in England (India drew the Test series 2-2 last summer in England). Have some patience with the team. We have a trend here. If you don't get a result that we want from the Indian team, then we go after it. Give them a break. They need to 'breathe out' as well. They are on the road continuously. So, give them some break. I'm sure that they'll get the right results for Team India. "Would it have made a difference if Ravindra Jadeja and Mohammed Siraj had played? "Time will tell. You say, what would have happened if Kapil paaji had played? I can't say much about what would have happened. But if he would have played, we would have talked about it. I can't really predict what would have happened if he would have played. If I would have known, I would have called Gautam and asked him to play," Harbhajan retorted.Talking about the ongoing 'Sandpaper-gate' controversy rearing its head in Australian cricket again, Harbhajan felt that it "wasn't a new thing" and that it showed that the Australian team sometimes received far more respect than they deserved."I don't think this is a new thing. This is a very old thing. Pakistan and India have been talking about this for a long time. That this is a reverse swing.We are making such a big thing about this. Australia was doing it before. England was doing it. South Africa was doing it. Wherever there is reverse swing, there must be something with the ball. People are doing it. How much they do it naturally, or the way they have done it with sandpaper, that is a little bad.Naturally, if you go to make the ball reverse, it takes some time to get the ball going. But if you make the ball reverse in the 10th over, then it is understood that there can be nothing but teasing."Australia is not as simple as they used to be. Their players are not as simple as they used to be. I have said this from day one, they should not be given so much respect. They should be given a lot of respect. They have also played the game. They have also done all these things. Now they have been caught or things have come out, they are saying that they did not know. It is not possible that you are living in one house, you are living in another house, you do not know who is living there. Everybody was part of it. I believe. If it is in the team, then it is a collective thing."
Article Summary: Harbhajan Singh has joined the chorus of those voicing their concern at the deteriorating player behaviour during India-Pakistan clashes. India's off-spin great has urged the game's authorities to "step in" to check the trend of players from both countries getting carried away in Indo-Pak cricket matches.

Article Title: BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships: Amid personal loss, Priya Sheoran hopes to make her mark
Article Text:
(From left) Bhartpreet Singh, Rahul Sarnaliya, Sadhna Ravi, Priya

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The past few months have tested Priya Sheoran in ways far beyond the athletics field.The Haryana discus thrower had been making frequent trips to hospital as her father Anup, a sub-inspector with Haryana Police and the man who inspired her to take up sports, had been unwell for several months. He passed away on Nov 10.Barely a fortnight later, Priya is set to step into the competition arena again, carrying both the grief of her loss and the hope of putting up a strong performance at the three-day inaugural BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships to be held at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar from Wednesday.“For the past four months, I had been going back and forth to the hospital with him. So, the preparation hasn’t been that good, but let’s hope for the best,” said Priya.The youngster, who has trained under celebrated discus thrower Seema Punia, won bronze at the U23 Asian Athletics Championships earlier this year, her first international medal.“It felt really good because it was my first international medal. This tournament is also being organised for the first time, so I’ll try to perform well here too and hopefully win a medal,” said the 22-year-old.Given what she has been through in recent months, Priya is trying not to burden herself with expectations.“I just want to put my best foot forward and give my best. I haven’t really thought about the result yet. I’ll go in with the mindset that I have to perform well,” she added.Priya will be among a 70-member Indian contingent looking to make an impression at the event.A little more than 200 athletes from six countries are expected to compete in the three-day event. With Thailand pulling out, athletes from Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Nepal and Sri Lanka will join hosts India in the competition.Among those attracting attention will also be 17-year-old sprinter Neil Samraj, who comes into the event on the back of a record-breaking season.Samraj broke the U18 national record in the 100m twice in a single day at the National Youth Athletics Championships in Ludhiana, eventually clocking 10.46s in the final. He lowered the mark further at the National Junior Athletics Championships in Chennai last month, running 10.45s. He also rewrote the U18 national record in the 200m in Chennai with a time of 21.03 seconds.Now, with an opportunity to test himself against athletes from the region, Samraj wants to see where he stands at the end of a long season.“Competing internationally will help me gain experience and prepare for many more international competitions where I will be up against athletes from different countries,” Samraj said in a social media post released by the Athletics Federation of India.“The plan is just to go hard because this is a very good opportunity to participate in a regional international competition. It will also help me understand where I stand and what kind of timings I can produce towards the end of the season.”For India’s young athletes, the championships provide another international opportunity at the end of a season that has witnessed several national records tumble. For Priya, however, simply returning to the throwing circle after a difficult few months will carry a significance of its own.
Article Summary: Priya Sheoran to compete at BIMSTEC U23 Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar. Haryana discus thrower will be carrying the grief of her father's death. Priya won bronze at the U23 Asian Athletics Championships earlier this year.

Article Title: Akash Deep steals the show as New Zealand finish Day 1 of 2nd Test at 246/5
Article Text:
India's Akash Deep celebrates the wicket of New Zealand's Rachin Ravindra

Akash Deep emerged as India's standout bowler on the opening day of the second Test against New Zealand, producing two outstanding deliveries in the post-lunch session to overshadow even the impressive Jasprit Bumrah . New Zealand, however, recovered towards the end of the day to finish at 246/5 after 85 overs at Hagley Oval in Christchurch on Friday.The two teams shared the honours, with New Zealand enjoying the first and final sessions while India fought back strongly in the middle session.After winning the toss and electing to bowl, India initially struggled to make inroads as New Zealand captain Tom Latham and Devon Conway put together a 77-run opening partnership. The hosts appeared comfortable against India's four-pronged pace attack before debutant Gurnoor Brar provided the breakthrough with the final delivery before lunch.Brar, who returned figures of 1/52 from 19 overs, dismissed Conway for 31 to give India some momentum heading into the break.However, it was Akash Deep who changed the complexion of the contest after lunch. The Bengal pacer, who returned to international cricket following a lengthy rehabilitation period for a lower back stress injury, finished with figures of 2/52 from 21 overs and was arguably India's most threatening bowler.Operating with the semi-new Kookaburra ball, Akash produced two superb deliveries to remove the well-set Latham and Rachin Ravindra, both caught behind by Rishabh Pant.Latham, who had scored 59, was beaten by a delivery that pitched on a good length before straightening just enough to take the outside edge. Ravindra, meanwhile, managed just eight deliveries at the crease before another testing delivery from Akash found his edge, with Pant completing the catch.In between those dismissals, Anshul Kamboj, whose selection had attracted considerable debate, accounted for Henry Nicholls. The left-hander departed for 16, leaving New Zealand in trouble at 110/4 after having reached 77 without losing a wicket. Kamboj returned figures of 1/56 from 17 overs.With India sensing an opportunity to take control, Tom Blundell and Daryl Mitchell joined forces to stabilise the innings. The pair added 74 runs for the fifth wicket before Washington Sundar broke the partnership, having Mitchell caught by Dhruv Jurel at leg-slip for 31. Washington finished with 1/36 from nine overs.Blundell remained unbeaten on 53 off 117 deliveries, displaying considerable patience during a challenging phase for the hosts. He found an able partner in Glenn Phillips, who continued New Zealand's recovery with an unbeaten 36 off 64 balls. The duo added 62 runs without being separated for the sixth wicket, ensuring the hosts finished the day on a relatively comfortable note.While Akash's ability to extract movement off the surface made him India's most effective bowler, Brar also made a positive impression on his Test debut. His inclusion appeared to add greater bite to the attack, with the debutant looking considerably more incisive than Prasidh Krishna.The Hagley Oval surface offered assistance to both batters and bowlers. There was bounce, carry and seam movement for the pacers, but batters who got themselves in were also able to play their shots and find value through the off-side.Earlier, Bumrah had a chance to strike in the opening over itself when Latham was given out leg-before. However, the New Zealand skipper successfully overturned the decision through DRS, avoiding a third successive duck. Bumrah went wicketless, but maintained impressive control throughout his spell, conceding just 37 runs in 19 overs.New Zealand were cautious during the initial exchanges, but batting became considerably easier once the first hour had passed. Conway, who had initially adopted a watchful approach, opened up with a stylish off-drive against Akash before following it up with a flashy cut for another boundary in the pacer's next over.Brar was introduced into the attack in the 18th over and immediately brought additional pace and bounce into the contest. The opening pair reached their 50-run partnership in the 19th over and looked largely untroubled against India's pace battery.Just when New Zealand appeared to be building a substantial opening stand, Akash and Brar combined to turn the tide, giving India a foothold in the contest before Blundell and Phillips ensured the hosts finished the opening day on level terms.
Article Summary: New Zealand finish day on 246-5 after 85 overs at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. India bowler Akash Deep took two wickets in the post-lunch session. Tom Blundell and Glenn Phillips added 62 runs for the sixth wicket.

NEW DELHI: Mohammed Siraj appeared visibly emotional after being left out of India's playing XI for the second Test against New Zealand in Christchurch. The Indian fast bowler was spotted covering his eyes with sunglasses as cameras captured him on the opening morning at Hagley Oval.The visuals caught the attention of former India batter Ajinkya Rahane and ex-spinner Murali Kartik , who were on live commentary. Both spoke about Siraj's reaction, with Kartik suggesting that the decision to drop him would have hurt the pacer.Siraj's omission has also raised questions, especially considering his record in the ongoing World Test Championship (WTC) cycle.Rahane was quick to notice Siraj covering his eyes with his sunglasses when the visuals appeared during the broadcast."These visuals," Kartik said before Rahane asked, "Is he crying?"Kartik agreed that the fast bowler looked upset and explained that players react differently when they are left out of the team. He felt Siraj was someone who always wanted to be on the field and give his best."I don't know, brother. Article Title: Cricket Australia gives players six weeks to share accounts of 2018 ball-tampering scandal
Article Text:

Cricket Australia (CA) has made public the terms of reference for its independent forum examining the events surrounding the controversial 2018 South Africa tour, which became infamous for the ball-tampering scandal. The six-week exercise will give players and support staff who were part of the tour an opportunity to share their experiences, although individual accounts will remain confidential and will not be made available to the CA Board.The board will instead receive a report summarising the key issues raised during the process, along with recommendations. The document will not include individual testimonies or any supporting material. CA has also committed to releasing the complete report, together with its response, within 30 days of receiving it.The independent exercise will be overseen by senior counsel Fiona McLeod AO SC, who will conduct private sessions with those willing to participate. The forum was announced following fresh revelations surrounding the 2018 scandal in Usman Khawaja's autobiography,In the book, Khawaja claimed that awareness of the sandpaper plan extended beyond the three players who were sanctioned by CA. David Warner and Cameron Bancroft have supported parts of his account, while Pat Cummins and several other bowlers have maintained that they had no knowledge of the plan.The forum will examine Australia's ball-management practices during the 2017-18 season, the team's involvement in all four Tests of the South Africa tour, and the incident involving Bancroft during the third Test in Cape Town on March 24, 2018. It will also look into CA's subsequent investigation into the episode.However, the exercise is not intended to reopen the original investigation or establish individual responsibility for the incident.CA has extended invitations to all players and support staff who were part of the South Africa tour, along with the management officials and board directors who were associated with the organisation at the time. Participants will be able to share their accounts through face-to-face or online meetings with McLeod, submit written statements or provide relevant documents.Taking part in the process is voluntary, and those who choose to participate will be permitted to have a support person or legal representative present.The terms of reference also lay down safeguards to protect the confidentiality of participants. Information shared by one individual cannot be attributed to them when seeking clarification from another participant unless they provide consent. Those involved will be informed about who can access their submissions and will have the opportunity to verify their own accounts for accuracy.In addition, the forum will be given access to the 2018 Culture and Governance Review of Australian Cricket conducted by The Ethics Centre, along with other relevant records and documents it considers necessary.CA Chair David Boon said the organisation was grateful to McLeod for agreeing to lead the initiative, which has been designed to provide a platform for everyone involved in the tour to share their experiences.“We’re grateful to Fiona McLeod AO SC for agreeing to lead the Independent Forum which has been designed to give voice to all the players and staff on the 2018 Test tour of South Africa," Boon said.“This is an opportunity to provide their accounts in a safe environment and to provide the CA Board with relevant information including about the events of that tour and resultant investigation.“We are acutely aware of the enormous toll the renewed focus on this tour eight years ago has had on those involved and their welfare remains our main priority.“This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn.“Publishing the report in full is part of our commitment to transparency, and to be open with cricket fans about what we learn.“It is also very important to understand that it will not seek to sanction or recriminate.”
Article Summary: Cricket Australia has made public the terms of reference for its independent forum examining the events surrounding the controversial 2018 South Africa tour. The six-week exercise will give players and support staff an opportunity to share their experiences, although individual accounts will remain confidential. The forum will examine Australia's ball-management practices during the 2017-18 season, and the incident involving Bancroft during the third Test in Cape Town on March 24, 2018.

MI Emirates registered their second win of ILT20 Season 5 after beating Abu Dhabi Knight Riders by 36 runs at the Zayed Cricket Stadium on Thursday. Sherfane Rutherford produced a stunning batting display, scoring 51 off just 18 balls, while Nicholas Pooran remained unbeaten on 42 off 33 deliveries. Their efforts helped MI Emirates post a massive 207/4 in 20 overs.The bowlers then stepped up to restrict the Knight Riders to 171/7. Fazalhaq Farooqi and Zahoor Khan picked up two wickets each, while Rashid Khan kept things tight with figures of 1/13. Sunil Narine was the standout bowler for the Knight Riders, taking 1/11, including a maiden.After being asked to bat first, MI Emirates got off to a flying start. Openers Kusal Perera and Muhammad Waseem attacked the bowling and added 77 runs for the first wicket in 52 balls.Perera scored 33 off 23 balls, while Waseem contributed 41 off 37 deliveries. The opening pair helped MI Emirates reach 57 without loss in the powerplay.Sunil Narine provided the Knight Riders with their first breakthrough in the ninth over when he dismissed Perera, who was caught behind.Abdullah Tarakhail, making his ILT20 debut, then struck twice to bring his team back into the contest. The Afghanistan pacer removed Waseem and Tajinder Singh (10 off 8), leaving MI Emirates at 124/3.The scoring rate slowed down for a while, with MI Emirates managing just one run in the 17th over. However, Rutherford and Pooran changed the momentum with some powerful hitting.The pair collected 17 runs each in the 18th and 19th overs to take the score to 177/3.Rutherford then took the attack to Knight Riders captain Jason Holder in the final over. He smashed three consecutive sixes off the first three deliveries to bring up his half-century in just 17 balls. However, he was caught on the fourth delivery.Kieron Pollard joined Pooran in the middle and made an immediate impact, hitting two more sixes. He scored 12 off just two balls as MI Emirates finished with a massive 207/4.Holder had an expensive outing, conceding 62 runs in his four overs. The last three overs alone cost the Knight Riders 64 runs.Chasing 208, Abu Dhabi Knight Riders began aggressively and collected 17 runs from Farooqi's opening over.However, the MI Emirates pacer bounced back quickly. He bowled Andre Fletcher (16 off 12) in the third over before dismissing Gulbadin Naib (5 off 6) in the fifth. The Knight Riders were reduced to 50/2.Zahoor Khan then removed Finn Allen (26 off 21) in the eighth over to put further pressure on the home team.Alishan Sharafu and Moeen Ali tried to revive the chase with a 45-run partnership off 27 balls. Both batters scored 36 runs, but Rashid Khan broke the stand by bowling Sharafu in the 13th over.Zahoor returned to dismiss Moeen in the 16th over, making the chase even tougher for the Knight Riders.Sunil Narine (4 off 15) retired out on the final ball of the 17th over. Andre Russell (6 off 3) was then bowled by Chris Jordan in the 18th over.Jason Holder (14 off 8) and Tarakhail (11 off 7) added some late runs, but the Knight Riders could only manage 171/7 in their 20 overs.Player of the Match Sherfane Rutherford spoke about his conversations with Kieron Pollard and Nicholas Pooran during the innings."(Kieron) Pollard and I had a chat about how you have more time than you think, and Pooran and I spoke about taking it deep. We were looking at 179-180, but the last two overs changed the game. I enjoyed it a lot, and I didn't realise it was three sixes in a row. It was good of Pollard to come in and finish it off."Abu Dhabi Knight Riders captain Jason Holder admitted that his team did not play well enough and failed to finish the bowling innings strongly."We were outplayed and a little flat. We bounced back nicely in the middle phase of our bowling innings but lost it at the back end. It's about executing better with bat and ball, and we didn't take a couple of chances early. We are a lot better than what we showed today, and I'm not worried. We'll assess when we review the game, and I wouldn't change anything I did today."MI Emirates: 207/4 in 20 overs (Sherfane Rutherford 51, Nicholas Pooran 42*, Muhammad Waseem 41; Sunil Narine 1/11, Abdullah Tarakhail 2/44).Abu Dhabi Knight Riders: 171/7 in 20 overs (Alishan Sharafu 36, Moeen Ali 36, Finn Allen 26; Zahoor Khan 2/38, Fazalhaq Farooqi 2/43).Player of the Match: Sherfane Rutherford.

India came roaring back with a superb spell of fast bowling in the second Test against New Zealand at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. After creating several chances without success, the Indian bowlers finally found their rhythm and picked up three wickets in the space of three overs.The sudden burst put New Zealand on the back foot, with Shubman Gill's decisions paying off. Akash Deep was the star of the spell, taking two wickets, while Anshul Kamboj also made an important contribution.India were looking for a breakthrough at the drinks break after New Zealand reached 106/1 at the end of 39 overs. The visitors had come close on several occasions but had little to show for their efforts.There were missed run-out opportunities, a DRS call that did not go their way and a few edges and top-edges that failed to bring wickets. The ball was still moving off the surface, but the Indian bowlers were unable to make the most of it.Akash Deep eventually gave India the much-needed breakthrough in the 42nd over by dismissing New Zealand captain Tom Latham. The left-hander had made 59 off 128 deliveries before a brilliant delivery ended his stay.Akash Deep bowled a good-length delivery outside off stump. The ball came in initially before holding its line, forcing Latham to play at it.He managed only a faint outside edge, which was safely collected by wicketkeeper Rishabh Pant.The dismissal lifted the Indian team's spirits after a frustrating period in which they had struggled to break through.India did not have to wait long for another wicket. In the following over, Anshul Kamboj sent Henry Nicholls back for 16 off 46 balls.Kamboj bowled a short delivery, prompting Nicholls to attempt a pull shot. The batter was early into the stroke and could only manage a top edge. Akash Deep made no mistake at long leg to complete the catch.Akash Deep then delivered another beauty to dismiss Rachin Ravindra for a duck and complete a remarkable spell for India.Coming from around the wicket, the pacer got the ball to move in with the angle before taking it away off the seam. Ravindra went forward to defend but edged it to Pant, who took his second catch of the spell.In the space of three overs, New Zealand had gone from 110/1 to 110/4, giving India a big opportunity to take control of the match.Even after picking up three quick wickets, the Indian bowlers kept creating problems for the New Zealand batters. However, Tom Blundell managed to survive a series of close calls.In the 45th over, Kamboj produced a big inswinger that struck Blundell on the pads. India appealed loudly for LBW, but Gill decided not to take a review after consulting the bowler. The delivery appeared to be going down the leg side.Blundell had another close escape against Gurnoor Brar in the 47th over. The pacer bowled a delivery at 136 kmph that pitched on off stump before moving away sharply. It beat Blundell's outside edge and went just over the off bail.Bumrah then thought he had Blundell trapped in front in the 48th over. After a discussion with Gill, India decided to review the umpire's decision.The pacer bowled a delivery that came back in sharply and beat Blundell's inside edge before hitting him on the back thigh. However, the ball-tracking showed that the delivery was going over the middle stump.India lost another review, while Blundell survived yet another testing moment against the Indian pace attack.
Article Summary: Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj take three wickets in three overs. Tom Blundell survives multiple close calls for New Zealand. New Zealand reach 106/1 at the drinks break in Christchurch. India lost another review in the 48th over as New Zealand fought back.

Article Title: IND vs NZ | Standing up to 140kph: How wicketkeepers are turning an old tactic into an attacking weapon
Article Text:
AP Photo

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From Alex Carey standing up to Scott Boland in the Ashes to Tom Blundell doing it against Matt Henry in England and at the Basin Reserve last week and Rishabh Pant employing the ploy in the first Test, wicketkeepers are increasingly prepared to stand up even when the ball is arriving at 130-140kph.Beyond the obvious courage required, the keeper is increasingly becoming a thief of the batter’s space.Former India wicketkeeper Chandrakant Pandit believes it is a response to how batting has evolved in the post-T20 era. “Today’s batters, even in Tests, have the courage to step out against pace. There is no fear about coming out of the crease to counter movement,” Pandit told TOI from Mohali, where he is coaching Madhya Pradesh in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy.“So the keeper standing up is basically an attempt to counter that and prevent the batter from advancing.”There is evidence that it works. Data from New Zealand’s 2026 series in England showed England averaging 25.36 against pace with Blundell back, but only 15.26 when he stood up.Henry explained why the Kiwis did it at the Basin for a long period of time. “The only mode of dismissal at the Basin was to bring the wickets into play and be prepared to look boring.Putting the ball outside off wasn’t going to help as there wasn’t a lot of carry.”India bowling coach Morne Morkel , though, remains unconvinced. “I’m old school. I like a bit of pace and bounce, balls carrying through to second and third slip, and getting your dismissals that way,” he said on Thursday.Pandit feels if a batter stands a yard outside his crease, he can alter the length at which the bowler wants to operate.“When the bowler alters his length, he can also compromise his swing,” he said. “If the wicketkeeper comes up, it puts the batter in two minds. He may want to play a delivery on the front foot, but with the keeper standing up, he might instead play it off the back foot.”That hesitation can bring bowled and lbw into play without the keeper ever touching the ball.At The Oval, Blundell stood up for most of Henry’s 24 overs despite the seamer operating around 135kph. All five wickets in Henry’s first-innings five-for came with Blundell up.For Pandit, that deserves admiration. “The wicketkeeper has to have a lot of courage to stand up at this sort of pace. It means he believes in his skills and is fearless.”Better protective equipment has helped. “You have helmets now. I don’t remember us wearing helmets while keeping, even on turning tracks or bad wickets. The quality of protective equipment is much better today. But equipment alone cannot give you courage. You still have to believe you can do it.”Pandit remembers Sunil Gavaskar once asking him to stand up to Raju Kulkarni in domestic cricket. “I started sweating,” he laughs. Gavaskar, he says, was employing some reverse psychology, possibly trying to suggest to the quick that he wasn’t bowling fast enough. Ramakant Desai would also ask Pandit to stand up in club cricket, hoping to create leg-side stumping opportunities off his inswingers.The tactic carries obvious risks: less reaction time and the possibility of conceding byes. But Pandit believes teams will accept the trade-off. “The idea is to disturb the batter. Tactically, you take that chance.”Learning the skill, however, requires sustained drills.“I would start with a tennis ball, hit with a racket from eight or 10 yards so the keeper can work on his reflexes,” he said. “The first thing is to get the fear out of his mind. Then progress to a hard ball with somebody throwing, and after that the bowling machine.”And repetition counts more than reputation.“No matter how good you are, you still need to practise. If Rishabh Pant is going to stand close to the stumps, he would definitely have practised it.”
Article Summary: Former India wicketkeeper Chandrakant Pandit believes it is a response to how batting has evolved in the post-T20 era. Pandit remembers Sunil Gavaskar once asking him to stand up to Raju Kulkarni in domestic cricket.

Article Title: Best ever! From 14 medals to 114: How India achieved more with fewer athletes at the Asian Para Games
Article Text:
Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

From 14 medals to 114: India's remarkable rise

India's Asian Para Games record

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Smaller contingent, bigger return

Hangzhou vs Aichi-Nagoya

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Athletics powers India's medal surge

India's leading medal-winning sports in Asian Para Games 2026

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Multiple medallists underline India's depth

Paralympic progress provides the wider context

Fourth place sets a new benchmark

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, India’s remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece.India’s campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally.But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event.The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings.More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years — from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations.India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally.At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals — one gold, four silver and nine bronze — to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings.The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth.Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth.Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth.The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth.The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough.The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals.India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals.The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged.On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports.Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success; it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport.Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish.Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total.Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze.Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals.Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals.That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions.India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports.Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul.Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds.Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally.The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad.India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport.At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals — five gold, eight silver and six bronze — lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th.The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings.India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving.China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold.India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze.The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games.The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines.For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport — one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi- Nagoya. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place. It is the best finish in the country's history at the event.

Article Title: Asian Para Games bronze leaves Suhas Yathiraj hungry for gold amid IAS duties and badminton
Article Text:
Suhas Yathiraj (Image credit: Instagram)

Third Paralympics, one big dream: Gold at LA 2028

Suhas Yathiraj (Image credit: Special arrangement)

IAS officer by day, shuttler by night

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Suhas Yathiraj (Image credit: Instagram)

Lee Chong Wei 's influence

NEW DELHI: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. Having beaten Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan in their group match just days earlier, the Indian shuttler had hoped to reach the final and fight for gold.Suhas lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23-21, 8-21, 15-21. He had chances to take the opening game but failed to convert them. After bouncing back to win the second game 21-8, he lost focus at a crucial stage of the decider.“Definitely not satisfied with bronze. I think if I had played up to my full potential, I would have definitely done better. In fact, I defeated Fredy of Indonesia in the group match in Nagoya only a few days ago,” Suhas told TimesofIndia.com from Aichi-Nagoya in Japan.“In the semifinal match, the first set was very close. I lost 23-21 and I had game point, set point, but I couldn't convert that. In the second set, I won very easily. In the third set, I think after 10-all, I sort of lost focus for two to three rallies. That is where he took the game. So, it was not my best day, I would assume. I would always love to win a gold medal. So, yes, I am a little sad from that angle,” he said.The defeat also reminded him of how important it is to perform under pressure at major tournaments.“It is the most important factor to win medals at major games because you might be training well, you might actually have the fitness and the skills. But if you don't recreate that during the major games, then probably it is of not much use in terms of professional success,” Suhas said.Suhas, an IAS officer, said he had never imagined representing India in international badminton a decade ago.In November 2016, he made his debut at the Asian Championships in Beijing and won gold. Since then, he has won several medals at major international events. These include bronze at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, silver at the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics, another silver at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, gold at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games and bronze in Nagoya.The 43-year-old has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024, winning silver on both occasions.With the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics approaching, the big question is whether he can go one step further and win gold.The desire is there, but Suhas is not looking too far ahead. He wants to take things one step at a time.“If you had asked me 10 years ago, I didn't even know that I would play for India. But whenever I look at the medals and the love I have got from fans and sportspersons around the world, the journey has been quite satisfying. I have had the honour of wearing the Indian jersey and winning medals for my country,” he said.“I am grateful for what God has given me. I never imagined that I would become an IAS officer one day, an Arjuna awardee or a badminton player winning medals for India. I never imagined all this. But thanks to the Almighty for all these,” Suhas, who is also an Arjuna Award recipient, said.“So if God and destiny have been kind to me, I hope they will take me to a place that I deserve. I hope I can do the best that I can in whatever I choose to,” he added.For most people, the end of a hectic working day is a time to relax, spend time with family, play with their children or watch a movie.For Suhas, it is often time to pick up his badminton racket and head to the court. His day includes early-morning gym sessions, office work, inspections, meetings, video conferences and checking files. Despite his demanding responsibilities as an IAS officer, he makes time for badminton and follows a strict fitness routine to compete at the highest level.Balancing the two careers is not easy, but his love for the sport keeps him going.“If you choose what you love, then the journey becomes painless. You enjoy that journey. That's what I do,” Suhas said.Explaining how he manages his work and training, he said: “It is challenging. My training generally starts in the night and it always involves sacrifices. Probably others would be spending time with their family members or having leisure time. My leisure time is to play badminton. In badminton, you need an extremely high level of fitness. It's challenging, hectic but at the same time I love it.”“I don't remember eating sweets in the last many months. I can't recall when I had my last sweet. So, I almost don't eat sweets or fried food and am also quite conscious about the nutrition that I take,” he said.Suhas grew up watching Malaysian badminton great Lee Chong Wei and was inspired by his movement on the court.“Yes, I have always been inspired by so many top players in the able-bodied category. Growing up, I watched the matches of Lee Chong Wei and how he used to move around the court,” he said.“Even in India, the top shuttlers perform extremely well, whether it is Lakshya Sen, HS Prannoy or Kidambi Srikanth. I know them personally and have always admired how well they are able to compete at the top,” Suhas signed off.
Article Summary: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. The Indian shuttler lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23- 21, 8-21, 15-21. Suhas has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024.

NEW DELHI: India signed off from the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games with their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals as the week-long continental competition concluded with a closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday.Double gold medallists Nishad Kumar and Mona Agarwal led the Indian contingent as flag-bearers at the ceremony, marking the end of a landmark campaign in which the country's para-athletes delivered historic victories, world-record performances and podium sweeps across disciplines.India finished fourth in the overall standings with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, surpassing its previous best of 108 medals at the 2022 Hangzhou Games.Held in Japan for the first time, the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games brought together around 4,000 athletes and staff from 45 countries and regions. The competition featured 18 sports, with more than 20 world records reportedly set during the seven-day event.China topped the medal table with 435 medals, including 207 gold, while hosts Japan finished second with 186 medals — 64 gold, 60 silver and 62 bronze.Uzbekistan emerged as the third-ranked nation, collecting 145 medals, including 45 gold.India's fourth-place finish was particularly significant given the size of its contingent. A total of 168 para-athletes represented the country at Aichi-Nagoya, compared with 309 at the previous edition in Hangzhou.President Droupadi Murmu congratulated the Indian contingent on its record performance, saying the achievement reflected the athletes' hard work, perseverance and self-belief.In a post on X, Murmu said the unprecedented medal haul would inspire young people to dream big, work with dedication and remain positive in the face of challenges. She also extended her congratulations to the entire Indian contingent.Para athletics was India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. Para badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze.India also won 11 medals in para swimming, seven in para table tennis, six in para archery and five in para shooting. The contingent added two medals each in para judo and para powerlifting.The closing ceremony brought together athletes, officials and dignitaries to mark the conclusion of the Games. Asian Paralympic Committee president Majid Rashed declared the event closed, highlighting the growing strength of para sport across Asia and its role in building a more inclusive society.Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also praised the athletes' determination, teamwork and sportsmanship, describing their performances as a reminder of the “profound beauty” of para sports.The Asian Para Games began in Guangzhou, China, in 2010, evolving from the Far East and South Pacific Games Federation for the Disabled. The Aichi-Nagoya edition was the fifth staging of the event, with Doha, Qatar, scheduled to host the sixth in 2030.For India, the closing ceremony marked the end of a historic campaign — one that raised the country's medal benchmark and showcased the depth and growing strength of its para-sport movement.

NEW DELHI: India's para-athletes produced a spectacular finish to their campaign at the Asian Para Games, registering their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals, including 30 gold, after a record-breaking final-day flourish in Aichi-Nagoya on Friday.India collected nine gold medals on the day — their biggest single-day haul of the ongoing edition — with champions emerging from badminton, archery, shooting and athletics. The country's final tally of 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze surpassed its previous best of 108 medals, including 27 gold, achieved at the Hangzhou Games in 2023.The achievement was particularly significant as India competed with a contingent of 168 athletes, nearly half the size of the squad that represented the country in Hangzhou.India remained fourth in the standings at the end of its campaign, although the final positions could change after a few remaining events on Saturday.Athletics remained India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals, 12 more than at the previous edition. On Friday, however, the spotlight was shared with a superb badminton campaign and gold-winning performances in shooting and archery. Star javelin thrower Sumit Antil led an Indian 1-2-3 finish in the men's F42-44/61-64 combined event . The reigning Paralympic and world champion threw 72.46m to defend his title, while Mahendra Gurjar took silver with 59.03m and Sandip Sanjay Sargar claimed bronze with 64.48m. Gurjar finished ahead of Sargar on Raza points, which determine rankings in combined-classification events.Pranav Soorma added another gold in the men's club throw F51, defending his title with a Games-record effort of 32.87m. Dharambir secured bronze with 27.71m.Sandeep delivered a world-record performance in the men's 400m T64, clocking 52.28 seconds for gold. India's Ajay Kumar also reached the podium, winning bronze in a Games-record time of 53.61 seconds.Haney produced another world record, throwing 60.49m to win the men's javelin F37/38 title. India also picked up silver medals through Nimisha Chakkungalparambil in the women's long jump T47 and Parmod Bijarnia in the men's 1500m T46, where he clocked 4:09.65.India's badminton contingent delivered three gold medals, led by Paris Paralympic champion Nitesh Kumar and Games debutant Naveen Sivakumar.Nitesh defeated compatriot and Tokyo Paralympic gold medallist Pramod Bhagat 21-18, 21-16 in the men's singles SL3 final. He later added a silver medal in mixed doubles SL3-SU5 alongside Thulasimathi Murugesan.Naveen, meanwhile, defeated Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan 21-9, 21-17 to win the men's singles SL4 title. Thulasimathi enjoyed a memorable campaign of her own , combining with Manasi Joshi to win gold in women's doubles SL3-SU5. The Indian pair beat China's Yang Qiuxia and Xiao Zuxian 21-16, 21-13 in the final.The 24-year-old also secured silver in women's singles SU5 after losing 18-21, 11-21 to Yang in the final, completing a three-medal haul.Shooter Mona Agarwal added another golden chapter to India's campaign, shattering the world record to win the women's 50m rifle 3 positions SH1 title with a score of 357.5 points.The 38-year-old had earlier won the women's 10m air rifle standing SH1 gold with a Games-record score of 250.0 points, edging compatriot Avani Lekhara, who took silver with 249.6.Mona's latest triumph gave her a second gold of the Games and further underlined her standing among India's leading para-shooters. She had also secured India's first 2028 Paralympic quota earlier this year.In archery, Paralympic champion Harvinder Singh teamed up with debutant Vijay Sundi to win the men's recurve doubles gold, defeating China's Yun Duo and Zhao Lixue 5-1 in the final.India's women's recurve doubles pair of Bhawna Choudhary and Pooja Jatyan settled for silver after losing 0-6 to China's Gao Zihan and Wang Xueqian.India's swimmers also exceeded expectations, finishing the Games with 11 medals, including three silver. Himanshu Nandal completed a hat-trick of bronze medals by finishing third in the men's 100m freestyle S11. The 22-year-old, who was born blind due to optic nerve failure, clocked 1:05.90, behind Japan's Uchu Tomita (58.22) and China's Chuanzhen Sun (58.70).Nandal had earlier won bronze in the men's 400m freestyle and 100m breaststroke S11 events. Ravi Budigina also finished with three medals, comprising two silver and one bronze.With nine gold medals on Friday and a record overall haul of 114, India signed off from its Asian Para Games campaign with its most successful performance at the continental event, surpassing the benchmark set in Hangzhou three years ago.

Article Title: Who is Himanshu Nandal? The para-swimmer who won a hat-trick of bronze medals at Asian Para Games in Japan

Who is Himanshu Nandal?

From Paris Paralympics qualification to Asian Para Games medals

NEW DELHI: Indian para-swimmer Himanshu Nandal made his mark at the Asian Para Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, completing a hat-trick of bronze medals with another podium finish in the men's 100m freestyle S11 event on Friday.The 22-year-old clocked 1 minute 5.90 seconds to finish third, behind Japan's Uchu Tomita, who won gold in a Games-record time of 58.22 seconds, and China's Chuanzhen Sun, who took silver in 58.70 seconds.Nandal's latest medal added to his earlier bronze finishes in the men's 400m freestyle and 100m breaststroke S11 events. He became one of India's standout performers in para swimming, matching compatriot Ravi Budigina's three-medal haul at the Games, which comprised two silver medals and a bronze.Born blind due to optic nerve failure, Nandal grew up in a sports-oriented family in Rohtak, Haryana. His father had played hockey at the national level, and sport became part of his life from an early age.At four, Nandal moved to Delhi and joined the National Association for the Blind, where he learnt Braille. He initially took up judo and went on to win medals at the national level before switching to swimming in 2021.The change opened a new chapter in his sporting journey, as he quickly progressed from domestic competitions to the international stage.Nandal achieved a significant milestone in 2024 when he became the first Indian blind swimmer to meet the Minimum Qualification Standard for the Paris Paralympics.A political science graduate from the University of Delhi's Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma College, he continued to build his experience against international opposition. In 2025, he reached two finals at the World Para Swimming Championships in Singapore.At the Asian Para Games, Nandal began his medal-winning run on Tuesday, clocking 5:10.91 to secure bronze in the men's 400m freestyle S11 event. He followed it up with another third-place finish in the 100m breaststroke before completing his hat-trick in the 100m freestyle on Friday.The S11 classification is for swimmers with visual impairment, including those with very low visual acuity or no light perception.Nandal's three-medal campaign in Japan marks another milestone in his progress as an Indian para-swimmer and adds to his growing experience at major international competitions.
Article Summary: Himanshu Nandal completes hat-trick of bronze medals at Asian Para Games 2026. The 22-year-old finished third in the men's 100m freestyle S11 event on Friday. Nandal is the first Indian blind swimmer to meet the Minimum Qualification Standard for the Paris Paralympics.
